title: The presidential salary pledge in the second term
summary: Trump has said repeatedly in his second term that he does not keep his $400,000 presidential salary. On August 6, 2025 he said his first paycheck went to the White House Historical Association, a private nonprofit. That association's October 27, 2025 statement, seen here only as a search excerpt, credits him with $66,000 of salary since January 2025. About $307,000 of salary had accrued by then, and roughly $729,000 had accrued by mid-November 2026. No donation in any later quarter is documented in public: the White House has not published quarterly announcements as it did in 2017-2020, and no agency has announced receiving one. The claim that he gives his salary away is therefore documented only in part. His first-term record is much fuller: at least about $1.4M of $1.6M is documented, with the last two quarters of 2020 unaccounted for. His recurring statement that he is the only president besides George Washington to donate his salary is false, because Herbert Hoover and John F. Kennedy also did.

sub_claims.statement: Trump has said he gives up his presidential salary in his second term.
sub_claims.finding: Before the term began, in the December 2024 Meet the Press interview, he said he would not accept the salary. On May 4, 2025, also on Meet the Press, he said he gives his entire salary back to the government. Asked whether he would also donate his crypto profits, he answered 'I never thought of that.' On August 6, 2025 he wrote on Truth Social that his first 'Paycheck' went to the White House Historical Association. In a May 2026 interview reported by the Washington Examiner, he said he gives 100% of the salary to White House preservation. At a Hispanic Heritage Month event at the White House on September 30, 2026 he said: 'In my first term, I donated it and I don't think I ever got a story about it ... But in my second term, I donated it, too.' He repeated the point in a post-election 60 Minutes interview in November 2026, as reported by FactCheck.org. These are his own statements, not records of payment.

sub_claims.statement: Each quarter's salary in the second term has been donated, with documented recipients and dates.
sub_claims.finding: Only one recipient is documented: the White House Historical Association (WHHA). It is a private 501(c)(3) nonprofit, not a federal agency. Trump's August 6, 2025 Truth Social post named it but gave no amount. The WHHA's October 27, 2025 statement, which mainly disputed a Wall Street Journal report about its role in the ballroom project, thanked the president for giving part of his salary to its work: $66,000 since January. That statement was seen only as a search excerpt and could not be opened. About $306,800 of gross salary had accrued between January 20 and October 27, 2025 (pro rata at $400,000 a year). The $66,000 is close to two months of gross pay ($66,667), but no source says which pay periods it covers, so that match is our own inference. No donation is documented for October 2025 onward, which covers Q4 2025 and Q1-Q3 2026. CNN's Daniel Dale reported in late September 2026 that Trump had not made public any evidence of donating his full second-term salary. Unlike 2017 to mid-2020, the White House has issued no quarterly donation announcements, and no agency has announced a gift.

sub_claims.statement: First-term comparison: Trump donated his salary quarterly to federal agencies.
sub_claims.finding:
From April 2017 to August 2020 the White House publicly announced quarterly gifts to federal agencies, often with a photo of the check. The documented recipients are as follows:
- Q1 2017: National Park Service, $78,333.32 (pro rata).
- Q2 2017: Education Department, $100,000.
- Later quarters: HHS (opioids), Transportation, Veterans Affairs, Small Business Administration, NIH's alcohol institute (NIAAA), Homeland Security, Agriculture and the Surgeon General's office.
- March and May 2020: HHS, for coronavirus work.
- Q2 2020: National Park Service, $100,000 (check dated July 13, 2020).
Fact-checkers place some of these in different quarters, so the per-quarter mapping varies between sources. Forbes found records for at least $1.4M of the $1.6M he earned. No record was found for July 2020 to January 20, 2021, and the White House, Treasury and OPM did not account for those months. In 2017 the White House initially declined to release documentation.

sub_claims.statement: By law the president is paid $400,000 a year plus allowances.
sub_claims.finding: 3 U.S.C. 102 sets the salary at $400,000 a year, paid monthly, at about $33,333 gross a month. The rate has been in effect since January 20, 2001, after the 1999 increase from $200,000. The same section provides an expense allowance of up to $50,000 a year for official duties. CRS describes that allowance as non-taxable, with any unused part reverting to the Treasury. 3 U.S.C. 103 allows up to $100,000 a year for travel, spent at the president's discretion and accounted for by his own certificate. 3 U.S.C. 105 covers official entertainment and White House Office expenses, with amounts set in annual appropriations. A commonly cited $19,000 entertainment figure could not be confirmed. On leaving office, a president receives a pension equal to Executive Schedule Level I pay under the Former Presidents Act. Whether Trump draws the $50,000 expense allowance this term is not publicly documented. The statute text was not opened (govinfo and Cornell LII fetches failed); the figures come from search excerpts of the statute and the CRS report RS20115.

sub_claims.statement: Donating the salary is a pure cost to Trump, with no tax offset.
sub_claims.finding: The salary is taxable wages. A gift to a federal agency (IRC 170(c)(1)) or to a 501(c)(3) such as the WHHA can be claimed as a charitable deduction if he itemizes, subject to adjusted-gross-income caps, and an unused deduction carries forward. So a donation can offset the income tax on the salary in whole or in part. CNBC (2020) reported that tax experts saw this possibility. His first-term returns, released by the House Ways and Means Committee in December 2022, show about $2M of charitable deductions in 2017, a little over $500,000 in each of 2018 and 2019, and none in 2020. Tax experts quoted by CNBC and USA Today said the returns cannot show whether the deducted gifts were the salary donations. No second-term tax return is public, so whether he has claimed a deduction for the 2025 WHHA gift is unknown.

sub_claims.statement: Trump is the only president, possibly besides George Washington, to donate his salary.
sub_claims.finding: Herbert Hoover and John F. Kennedy both gave away their presidential salaries. George Washington initially declined pay but accepted the $25,000 salary. Trump repeated the claim on August 6, 2025, in May 2026 and again in a November 2026 interview, in which he added 'I don't know if that's right.' CNN's Daniel Dale also disputed his September 30, 2026 statement that his first-term donations never got press coverage: 'They were regularly covered when he announced them.'

corrections: Claimed: Trump donates his whole salary each quarter in his second term. The record shows one documented recipient (the White House Historical Association) and one documented total ($66,000 from January to October 27, 2025, according to the association). Nothing is documented for later quarters.
Claimed: the second-term salary goes to federal agencies, as in the first term. The record shows that the only documented second-term recipient is a private nonprofit, not a government agency.
Claimed: Trump is the only president besides Washington to give up his pay. The record shows that Hoover and Kennedy also did, and that Washington accepted his salary.

Claimed: the second-term donations total $400,000 (one aggregator's figure for the first paycheck). The record shows that pay is monthly at about $33,333 gross, and the recipient itself reports $66,000 through late October 2025.
denials_and_context: Trump's position: he has said repeatedly (May 2025, August 2025, May 2026, September 2026, November 2026) that he donates his salary, and that he gets no credit for it.

White House Historical Association: in its October 27, 2025 statement it thanked the president for contributing part of his salary ($66,000 since January). It did not respond to press requests for comment in August 2025. In its statements on the ballroom it disputed parts of a Wall Street Journal report about its role.

Critics: CNN's Daniel Dale said Trump has released no evidence of donating his full second-term salary. The Maddow Blog (MS NOW) and others argue that his disclosed 2025 income, at least about $2.2B by most counts (see C29), dwarfs the $400,000 salary. That is a comparison of scale, not evidence about the donations.

Context: the WHHA is a private nonprofit that funds White House acquisitions and preservation. Its ties to Trump's White House renovations, including a separate $2.5M gift linked to East Wing documentation, have been the subject of Washington Post reporting. Trump himself linked his salary gift to the renovations.

Context: in the first term, after declining at first in 2017, the White House published regular announcements and check photos. Even so, the final six months of first-term pay were never documented. A gap in announcements is not proof that no donation was made, and a statement of intent is not proof that one was.

leads.title: Trump gave White House aides cash gifts in 2025
leads.why_connected: White House financial disclosures reported by the Washington Post and Reuters (September 2026) show Trump personally gave aides including Natalie Harp, Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris about $45,000 each, and Walt Nauta about $20,000. That raises questions under the statute barring federal employees from supplementing their salaries, and it is money flowing out of Trump's pocket alongside the salary question.

leads.title: White House Historical Association's donors and its role in the ballroom and East Wing project
leads.why_connected: The association is the only documented recipient of Trump's second-term salary. The Washington Post (October 2026) reported that it took $2.5M from a donor who wanted the East Wing demolished and told staff not to discuss the gift. The association says none of that money went to the demolition or the ballroom.

leads.title: Whether the WHHA's 2025-2026 IRS Form 990 or annual report lists Trump's salary gifts
leads.why_connected: A 990 Schedule B (donor amounts, names usually redacted in public copies) or an annual report could corroborate or update the $66,000 figure and show any 2026 gifts. Not yet checked.
